01 / The challenge

A table carries a task, not just data.

A securities tool brings accounts, markets, positions, values and actions into a dense working surface. Visually similar controls can have very different consequences, so component boundaries cannot be based on appearance alone.

The aim was to reduce repeated interface construction while preserving business meaning. I researched component-library methods and business-unit decomposition with colleagues, then developed the relevant structures into components and guidelines.

Context

Which account?

Account and market context determine how the data should be understood.

State

What is happening?

Default, selected, hover and no-data states need distinct feedback.

Action

What can I do?

Each action belongs to a task and must retain its business meaning.

02 / Decomposition

Use business meaning to decide what can be shared.

For account positions, the table, account context and controls can become reusable units while keeping their relationships explicit. A shared structure only works when its meaning and behaviour match.

My responsibility included the relevant component design, usage specifications and ongoing maintenance. Where tasks have different rules, preserving those differences matters more than forcing consistency.

A component boundary is also a product-design decision.
03 / States

Let state change without moving the reading structure.

The source “Table / Account Positions” component includes default, selected, hover and no-data variants. Feedback needs to explain what changed while keeping information position and reading order stable.

The specification therefore addresses both appearance and behaviour across situations. Consistent state definitions also give maintenance work a shared reference.

INTERACTIVE DESIGN EXPLANATION

Change the state, keep the reading structure.

Query, select a row or switch theme. Each state keeps the same information structure.

04 / Specifications & maintenance

Share the structure; preserve the meaning of the action.

Buy, sell, confirm, cancel and input controls have related structures, but are not the same action. I maintained components and specifications to give repeated modules a consistent foundation while preserving these distinctions.

The components supported cross-project reuse and day/night theme adaptation. These experiences demonstrate a qualitative maintenance benefit; historical time savings were not measured.

05 / Outcome & reflection

A reusable design foundation starts with clear boundaries.

The delivery was Figma components, usage guidelines and maintenance. I contributed to the shared method research and business decomposition; software implementation was outside my responsibility.

To evaluate this approach further, I would compare repeated-module assembly time, omitted states and the effort needed to carry a change across instances. These measures would show more concretely whether reuse helps the team.
